newsitem.title: CROATIA: Bosnia, Croatia reaffirm right of refugees.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia, Croatia reaffirm right of refugees.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Bosnia's presidency chairman, Alija Izetbegovic, met straight-talking U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, who arrived in this Adriatic resort on Wednesday to try to speed up the Balkan peace process.
Prior to the meeting, Tudjman and Izetbegovic reaffirmed the right of all refugees in Bosnia to return home in safety without intimidation.
But Izetbegovic told reporters he and the Croatian leader had overestimated the pace at which refugee returns could be achieved.

Their summit was held at old villa in Split. Before going into the talks with Holbrooke, who is the architect of the Bosnian peace agreement reached in Dayton, Ohio, at the end of 1995, Izetbegovic and Tudjman signed a joint statement.

In it, they pledged to strengthen the political independence of Bosnia-Hercegovina and said they would draw up an agreement outlining relations between the two countries which would "further cooperation". They plan to exchange the agreement by September 1.

Izetbegovic said there had been "positive trends" with the return of refugees in Bosnia and made no reference to events this weekend in the central Bosnian town of Jajce when hundreds of Moslem refugees fled their homes in fear under intimidation from angry, drunken Bosnian Croat mobs.
They had returned to their pre-war homes in the area in recent weeks and said after leaving that they planned to return once again.
International organisations in Sarajevo blamed local authorities and said it was up to them to protect returnees regardless of their ethnic background.
"I think we had overestimated the possibility of implementing something like the return of refugees, freedom of movement and punishment of war criminals," Izetbegovic said.

"We have overestimated the pace at which it can go, but recently there have been some positive trends...there is a wave of returns in central Bosnia which shows some trends for the future," Izetbegovic said without mentioning Jajce.
"It is not just the question of Jajce, it is a very complex question and should be solved with goodwill and organisation so that there are no new conflicts," Tudjman told reporters.

The Croatian president has come under intense international pressure to strengthen his support of the Moslem-Croat Federation, formed in 1994 with the help of U.S. diplomacy, which makes up half of post-war Bosnia.
"The mutual commitment to preserve and strengthen the integrity, sovereignty and political independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was jointly affirmed," the statement said.

Holbrooke had timed his return to the Balkans to coincide with the summit and will later travel to Sarajevo and Belgrade. His visit comes as international pressure has increased in an effort to move the Bosnian peace process forward.

"International envoys are always welcome especially when it comes to implementing what has been agreed. Today we reached an agreement on our own but if necessary they will be called to come and help with its implementation," Izetbegovic told reporters.
Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of the presidency, and Tudjman have had stormy relations since leading their republics out of the old Yugoslav federation.
Tudjman was anxious to hold the meeting earlier to prove to the United States and Europe that he supported the Federation.

But Izetbegovic had declined to meet Tudjman for months until Zagreb made good on previous commitments. After coming under heavy Western pressure, Tudjman pushed the Bosnian Croats in Mostar into agreeing to have a unified police force last month.
Holbrooke told reporters on arrival at the airport it was clear progress was being made "but at much too slow a pace".
"We're here to encapsulate what has happened and try to accelerate the process and keep it moving forward," he said.

Tudjman and Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic have been criticised for failing to hand over suspected war criminals to The Hague, though Tudjman contends he has done more than Milosevic given their countries' respective roles in the war.

"The cooperation with the International Tribunal for War Crimes in The Hague will be continued," the statement said. "It is a joint conviction that proceedings and trials should reflect the level of involvement of sides and individuals."
